criteria.rationale: The kit's step transition is AnimatePresence mode="wait" keyed by step. For two consecutive steps that do not share a group, the outgoing scene fades out and unmounts before the incoming one mounts. With mode="wait" the incoming step is not mounted until the outgoing exit finishes, so both copies are never present together.

subcomponents.title: Verification tooling robustness

criteria.rationale: All four scripts (verify and inspect, repository and bootstrap copies) share one startPreview. It spawns `node node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js preview` directly through process.execPath, so the child is the Vite preview server itself, not an npm or npx wrapper. stopPreview sends SIGTERM to that child, awaits its 'exit' event (capped at 3s), then sends SIGKILL if it is still alive. Every script starts the preview and the browser inside a try whose finally runs `await browser?.close(); await stopPreview(preview?.child)`. Success, a failing check, a chromium() launch failure and any later error therefore all close the server. Repository verify returns early on build or sample failure before any preview starts. installSignalCleanup covers SIGINT and SIGTERM. Judge C fails this on two points, and neither decides the requirement. (1) The readiness-timeout branch in startPreview sends SIGTERM without awaiting. That path runs before the preview has started, so it is not one of the named post-start exit paths. It still signals the Vite server itself, not a wrapper. (2) The un-awaited SIGKILL escalation fires only if the server ignores SIGTERM for 3s. In that case the awaited cleanup has already been attempted and the forced kill goes to the server process itself. The requirement asks that the server, not a wrapper, be terminated and awaited on success, on browser launch failure and on post-start errors. Lines 50-55 and the finally blocks do exactly that. Judges A and B match this reading.

criteria.rationale: I found four delivered tests that drive a real browser. The vitest include list in vite.config.ts:9 covers src/**, tests/integration/** and tests/e2e/**, and the jsdom/testing-library tests under src (for example contracts.test.tsx) render in jsdom without a browser. Of the browser tests, three run the verify or inspect script: tests/e2e/verification.test.ts (execFileSync npm run verify), tests/e2e/verification-failures.test.ts (spawnSync verify with fault injection), and tests/integration/presentation-skill.test.ts (npm run verify in a fresh bootstrap). The fourth, INT-002 in tests/integration/inspection.test.ts, spawns the inspect script. None of these test files contains a fixed sleep, waitForTimeout, or immediate-return call treated as a wait. They run synchronous process calls and assert on the exit status and output. The only timer is the setTimeout at inspection.test.ts:86-89. It is a 10 s kill guard that rejects when the child process hangs, not a delay before an assertion. That test awaits the child's 'exit' event, which is observable state. Where the scripts these tests run drive the browser, every wait for a transition polls observable state. waitForStep (preview-utils.mjs:71-73) runs page.waitForFunction until data-step-index equals the wanted step, with a timeout. verify.mjs calls it at line 60 after each ArrowRight, before asserting the index (61-62). The present/browse toggles wait through waitForFunction on data-presentation-mode (49, 53). inspect-presentation.mjs:65 calls waitForStep before each capture. Judge C's reason does not decide the criterion. The guidance's fail case is a fixed wait used for a transition before asserting the step. In verify.mjs, waitForStep and checkOutline have already asserted the step (60-63) before page.waitForTimeout(100) at line 64. That 100 ms is a grace period for late console errors after the state check, not a substitute for waiting on the transition. In inspect-presentation.mjs:66, the --settle delay also comes after the state-based waitForStep. It is a user-configurable settle option, which INT-002 exercises on purpose (inspection.test.ts:31-39), and the guidance lists 'longer fixed settle delays' as validator noise. Both delays are in the verification scripts. Neither is a test that sleeps instead of waiting for state. Judges A and B reached the same pass.

criteria.rationale: The requirement is not met. The candidate chose to leave a substantial share of the specified user-visible behavior unexercised, and none of those omissions is environmental. 1) Requirement-003 has 14 scenarios (packet.txt:174-211). Seven were never exercised: 'Missing sample fails', 'Console or page error fails verification', 'Step error fails verification', 'Suspicious overlap is reported', 'Intentional overlap can be marked', 'Indistinct active chrome is reported' and 'Unpolished attribution is reported'. 'Clear outcome' was never observed through `npm run verify` either. The only observations recorded are a passing build and the inspection helper reporting no warnings on the clean sample (packet.txt:1215-1216, 1266). The helper was runnable in this environment. The test plan's own definitions of these behaviors (INT-002 warnings and exemptions at packet.txt:1512-1518; E2E-002 failure phases at packet.txt:1530-1536) show they are product command behaviors, not separate-agent skill journeys. The log says why it skipped them: the 'process-failure ... runs were not added' because they are 'owned by E2E-002/INT-001 and the automated-suite boundary excludes rerunning them' (packet.txt:1220), and fault injection is out of scope (packet.txt:1236, 1276-1277). That is a scope choice, not an environmental impediment. 2) The motion scenarios 'Persisting entity morphs', 'New entity enters after others settle' and 'Continuing entities are not faded as newcomers' (packet.txt:44-58) were checked only against a weaker property. The record shows only that DOM nodes stayed mounted and new nodes appeared (packet.txt:1208). It does not show morphing, newcomers waiting until continuing motion settles, or the absence of fades. The criterion says that kind of weaker check does not cover a scenario. AT-003 also names these motion outcomes explicitly (packet.txt:1568). Judges A and B treated these omissions as environmental or as a minority. The cited log lines attribute the verifier and warning omissions to the acceptance-suite boundary (packet.txt:1215, 1220, 1236), not to an unavailable agent. The criterion excuses only environmental impediments; a disclosed scope choice still counts against coverage. Together, half of requirement-003 plus the continuity motion scenarios is a substantial share of the specified behavior. Judge B also acknowledged that DOM persistence is weaker than motion sequencing. That fact decides the motion scenarios against coverage.
evidence: The requirement-003 inventory lists failure-reporting scenarios and four warning/overlap scenarios (packet.txt:174-211).
The stable-entity and grouped-scene scenarios require morphing, newcomers entering after others settle, and continuing entities not being faded (packet.txt:44-58).
The log's continuity check observed only DOM nodes remaining mounted and new nodes appearing (packet.txt:1208).
The log records that fault injection, advisory-warning fixtures and `npm run verify` were not exercised, citing the automated-suite exclusion (packet.txt:1215-1216, 1220, 1236, 1276-1277).
The test-plan definitions show that warning and verification-failure behaviors belong to the product's inspect and verify commands (packet.txt:1512-1518, 1530-1536).

The presentation-owned ENTITIES contract contains dead members, though. `ENTITIES.tray`, `ENTITIES.morph` and `ENTITIES.depth` are declared in entities.ts but never read anywhere in src. It also says to fail when a check converts a non-numeric hook into a number that still satisfies its comparison, and it names the first step as an example. scripts/verify.mjs:40-41 reads the first step's hook as `Number(await page.locator('[data-step-index]').first().getAttribute('data-step-index'))` and rejects only `actual !== 0`. An element that has the attribute but with an empty or whitespace value converts to 0. That passes the step-0 check, so a non-numeric hook is accepted as valid index 0. The waitForStep helper (scripts/preview-utils.mjs:72) has the same bare `Number(...) === index` comparison, with no integer or format check. Judge B's reason is borne out by these lines and decides the hook-validation clause, so I rule B's fail. Judges A and C correctly note several things: count must equal SAMPLE_OUTLINE.length (verify.mjs:37-38), so a missing, zero or NaN count fails. An absent attribute yields NaN for steps 1 and up. The browser-backed test files are tests/e2e/verification.test.ts, tests/e2e/verification-failures.test.ts, tests/integration/inspection.test.ts and tests/integration/presentation-skill.test.ts. The fixed waits the dissent relies on come after those state checks. In verify.mjs, page.waitForTimeout(100) runs after waitForStep, the index check and checkOutline, as a grace period for late console errors. In inspect-presentation.mjs, the user-configurable --settle delay runs after waitForStep, and the guidance lists longer fixed settle delays as validator noise. Neither replaces a wait for the step transition before the step is asserted, which is the fail case the guidance names. The dissent does not answer this majority reasoning.

result.rationale: The requirement is not met. The candidate chose to leave a substantial share of the specified user-visible behavior unexercised, and none of those omissions is environmental. 1) Requirement-003 has 14 scenarios (packet.txt:174-211). Seven were never exercised: 'Missing sample fails', 'Console or page error fails verification', 'Step error fails verification', 'Suspicious overlap is reported', 'Intentional overlap can be marked', 'Indistinct active chrome is reported' and 'Unpolished attribution is reported'. 'Clear outcome' was never observed through `npm run verify` either. The only observations recorded are a passing build and the inspection helper reporting no warnings on the clean sample (packet.txt:1215-1216, 1266). The helper was runnable in this environment. The test plan's own definitions of these behaviors (INT-002 warnings and exemptions at packet.txt:1512-1518; E2E-002 failure phases at packet.txt:1530-1536) show they are product command behaviors, not separate-agent skill journeys. The log says why it skipped them: the 'process-failure ... runs were not added' because they are 'owned by E2E-002/INT-001 and the automated-suite boundary excludes rerunning them' (packet.txt:1220), and fault injection is out of scope (packet.txt:1236, 1276-1277). That is a scope choice, not an environmental impediment. 2) The motion scenarios 'Persisting entity morphs', 'New entity enters after others settle' and 'Continuing entities are not faded as newcomers' (packet.txt:44-58) were checked only against a weaker property. The record shows only that DOM nodes stayed mounted and new nodes appeared (packet.txt:1208). It does not show morphing, newcomers waiting until continuing motion settles, or the absence of fades. The criterion says that kind of weaker check does not cover a scenario. AT-003 also names these motion outcomes explicitly (packet.txt:1568). Judges A and B treated these omissions as environmental or as a minority. The cited log lines attribute the verifier and warning omissions to the acceptance-suite boundary (packet.txt:1215, 1220, 1236), not to an unavailable agent. The criterion excuses only environmental impediments; a disclosed scope choice still counts against coverage. Together, half of requirement-003 plus the continuity motion scenarios is a substantial share of the specified behavior. Judge B also acknowledged that DOM persistence is weaker than motion sequencing. That fact decides the motion scenarios against coverage.

demo-integration.rationale: All nine step modules set groupKey 'reference-scene' and the same Scene. Stage keys its motion.div on groupKey plus the Scene name, so the key is identical across steps and the scene stays mounted. Only the payload changes. audit_results.rationale: The review guidance says the verifier must not treat a non-numeric data-step-index as progress. It says to fail when the check turns an absent or non-numeric hook into a number that still passes its comparison, and it gives the first step as an example. That means the guidance names this scenario, so it is not a hypothetical outside the criterion. scripts/verify.mjs:40 reads the first step's index with a bare Number(getAttribute('data-step-index')). Line 41 rejects only when actual !== 0, with no integer or format check. The locator '[data-step-index]' matches any element that has the attribute, whatever its value. An empty or whitespace value is non-numeric, but Number() turns it into 0, so it passes the step-0 check and counts as valid index 0. scripts/preview-utils.mjs:72 has the same bare Number(...) === index comparison. The things the other judges point to are real: the count must equal SAMPLE_OUTLINE.length, and the stalled-transition test exists. Neither deals with the non-numeric index on the first step, so the hook-validation clause is unmet.

first_results.rationale: None of the delivered test files contains a fixed sleep. E2E-001 runs verify with execFileSync and asserts only on its output. E2E-002 runs spawnSync of verify per injected fault, then asserts on exit status and output, with one bounded fetch to confirm cleanup. INT-002 runs spawnSync of inspect and asserts on output and artifacts. Its only setTimeout is a 10s kill guard around awaiting a child's 'exit' event, not a sleep before an assertion. In the browser driving these tests exercise, step advances wait on state: waitForStep is page.waitForFunction polling data-step-index, and present/browse toggles are waitForFunction on data-presentation-mode. audit_results.rationale: Both copies of preview-utils.mjs start the server with spawn(process.execPath, [node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js, 'preview', ...]). The child process is therefore the Vite preview server itself, not an npm or npx wrapper. stopPreview sends SIGTERM to that child and waits for its 'exit' event, capped at 3s, then sends SIGKILL if it is still alive. In all four scripts the preview starts inside a try block, and the browser launches inside the same block. Each finally block runs `await browser?.close(); await stopPreview(preview?.child)`. These four scripts are the repository verify (lines 26-73), repository inspect (lines 43-102), bootstrap verify (lines 1-38) and bootstrap inspect (lines 43-102). Success, a failing check, a chromium() launch failure and any error thrown after startPreview returns all pass through that cleanup. The bootstrap verify script runs its build and registry checks before the preview starts (lines 9-14). If readiness times out, startPreview sends SIGTERM to the Vite process without waiting for it. That happens before the preview is ready, and the signal still goes to the server itself, so no wrapper is left with a running server. The guidance names success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and later errors; this pre-readiness path is none of them. The SIGKILL is sent without waiting only if the server ignores SIGTERM for 3s, which the material does not show happening. Every exit path the requirement names is met in all four copies.

result.rationale: All four scripts (verify and inspect, repository and bootstrap copies) share one startPreview. It spawns `node node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js preview` directly through process.execPath, so the child is the Vite preview server itself, not an npm or npx wrapper. stopPreview sends SIGTERM to that child, awaits its 'exit' event (capped at 3s), then sends SIGKILL if it is still alive. Every script starts the preview and the browser inside a try whose finally runs `await browser?.close(); await stopPreview(preview?.child)`. Success, a failing check, a chromium() launch failure and any later error therefore all close the server. Repository verify returns early on build or sample failure before any preview starts. installSignalCleanup covers SIGINT and SIGTERM. Judge C fails this on two points, and neither decides the requirement. (1) The readiness-timeout branch in startPreview sends SIGTERM without awaiting. That path runs before the preview has started, so it is not one of the named post-start exit paths. It still signals the Vite server itself, not a wrapper. (2) The un-awaited SIGKILL escalation fires only if the server ignores SIGTERM for 3s. In that case the awaited cleanup has already been attempted and the forced kill goes to the server process itself. The requirement asks that the server, not a wrapper, be terminated and awaited on success, on browser launch failure and on post-start errors. Lines 50-55 and the finally blocks do exactly that. Judges A and B match this reading.

result.rationale: Verify checks the sample's titles, captions, outline order and registration against the rendered page at each step. It loads the sample route in Chromium and reads data-step-count from the DOM, requiring 9. An unregistered slug would render no step count, so registration is proven from the rendered route. checkOutline(step) reads innerText of [data-presentation-caption], [data-presentation-step-title] and, after toggling present mode, [data-presentation-title]. It compares each to SAMPLE_OUTLINE[step]. The loop presses ArrowRight, waits for data-step-index === step, and calls checkOutline at every one of the nine steps, so order is checked against what is rendered. Judge C fails this because assertCanonicalSample also reads source files. That pre-check uses String.includes and indexOf, not regular expressions; the requirement's fail clause is regex matching over source text. It is also an extra guard: every listed check is independently performed against the rendered page at each step. Judges A and B match this reading.

result.rationale: I found four delivered tests that drive a real browser. The vitest include list in vite.config.ts:9 covers src/**, tests/integration/** and tests/e2e/**, and the jsdom/testing-library tests under src (for example contracts.test.tsx) render in jsdom without a browser. Of the browser tests, three run the verify or inspect script: tests/e2e/verification.test.ts (execFileSync npm run verify), tests/e2e/verification-failures.test.ts (spawnSync verify with fault injection), and tests/integration/presentation-skill.test.ts (npm run verify in a fresh bootstrap). The fourth, INT-002 in tests/integration/inspection.test.ts, spawns the inspect script. None of these test files contains a fixed sleep, waitForTimeout, or immediate-return call treated as a wait. They run synchronous process calls and assert on the exit status and output. The only timer is the setTimeout at inspection.test.ts:86-89. It is a 10 s kill guard that rejects when the child process hangs, not a delay before an assertion. That test awaits the child's 'exit' event, which is observable state. Where the scripts these tests run drive the browser, every wait for a transition polls observable state. waitForStep (preview-utils.mjs:71-73) runs page.waitForFunction until data-step-index equals the wanted step, with a timeout. verify.mjs calls it at line 60 after each ArrowRight, before asserting the index (61-62). The present/browse toggles wait through waitForFunction on data-presentation-mode (49, 53). inspect-presentation.mjs:65 calls waitForStep before each capture. Judge C's reason does not decide the criterion. The guidance's fail case is a fixed wait used for a transition before asserting the step. In verify.mjs, waitForStep and checkOutline have already asserted the step (60-63) before page.waitForTimeout(100) at line 64. That 100 ms is a grace period for late console errors after the state check, not a substitute for waiting on the transition. In inspect-presentation.mjs:66, the --settle delay also comes after the state-based waitForStep. It is a user-configurable settle option, which INT-002 exercises on purpose (inspection.test.ts:31-39), and the guidance lists 'longer fixed settle delays' as validator noise. Both delays are in the verification scripts. Neither is a test that sleeps instead of waiting for state. Judges A and B reached the same pass.

The running page exposed nine steps; a nine-step sweep recorded indices 0–8, scene payload states 1–9, matching active progress indices, and all nine distinct expected captions in order. Project-local inspection also settled and captured all nine steps at both 1440×900 and 390×844. Production build succeeded and AXI reported no console messages.

- **Typed payload boundary and build contract:** The copied application passed `npm ci` and `npm run build` (TypeScript and Vite). Types themselves are compile-time behavior; the browser cannot show whether casts were used. The scenario was not tested with a separate authored typed presentation.

- **Stable entities, grouped persistence, newcomers and exits:** Between steps 1 and 2, the same scene DOM node and the same continuing person entity DOM node remained mounted; a new skill node and connector appeared; later steps added cards and the verification node. All nine sample states were visually traversed. **Limitation:** the committed sample intentionally accumulates entities and contains no departing entity, so the exit animation path could not be exercised using the approved reference presentation.

- **Browse/present chrome, mode preservation, attribution and brand:** Browse showed the multi-line caption, ToC at wide viewport, progress, and previous/next controls. Present showed the active step title and marker while hiding caption, ToC and previous/next controls. Button and `P` toggles preserved step index 8. Accessibility snapshot showed the “made by and-scene” link to `https://github.com/and-scene/and-scene`; no default top-left brand link appeared. Active progress/ToC entries exposed `aria-current="step"` and `data-active="true"`. **Finding F-01:** browse mode omits the active step title.

- **Keyboard, touch, direct navigation and boundaries:** Right, Space, PageDown advanced; Left and PageUp reversed. A focused Next button plus ArrowRight advanced only once (index remained 1 after the key), so the navigation listener did not double-handle the focused control. Synthetic horizontal touch events through AXI eval moved 1→2 on left swipe and 2→1 on right swipe. Progress selection moved to index 4 and showed active index 4; selecting “THE BUILD” jumped to its first step (index 5). Previous at index 0 stayed at 0; ArrowRight at index 8 stayed at 8.

- **Fixed canvas and visual composition:** Canvas element uses 880×380 dimensions; AXI observed a uniform transform scale of 0.443 at 390×844. Screenshots were reviewed for first, eighth (dense), and ninth (last) steps at wide and narrow viewports. Wide composition is readable with no visible chrome collisions. **Finding F-02:** diagram text is near-illegible after narrow uniform scaling. An additional 320×568 check (scale 0.364) showed the same issue more strongly.

- **Style-neutral kit and optional styling framework:** In the disposable preview, disabling both loaded stylesheets changed a presentation Box from a solid border, colored background and Space Grotesk to no border, transparent background, black text and browser-default Times New Roman. This supports that the kit supplies no fallback card treatment. Root dependencies contain no Tailwind.

This pass did not run a separate skill-agent dialogue in empty standalone and partial-monorepo projects, so the interactive exchange, actual target resolution, preservation and generated route outcomes were not independently observed. A second agent/user transcript is unavailable in this autonomous single-agent session.

- No full npm test, lint, or `npm run verify`; prohibited by the acceptance skill.
### INT-002: Screenshot helper emits faithful artifacts and advisory warnings
- Covers: Project-local screenshot capture, settled transitions, overlap exemptions, active-navigation diagnostics, and attribution diagnostics.
- Boundary: The project-local inspection script drives a production preview in Chromium and writes screenshots plus diagnostics to the filesystem.

- Setup: Use a controlled registered test presentation with multiple steps and variants containing an unmarked text collision, an explicitly allowed overlap, indistinct active chrome, and unpolished attribution.
- Action: Run the inspection helper through every step after the configured settle interval.

- Assertions: One predictable screenshot is written per step; captures occur only after transitions settle; the unmarked collision, indistinct active state, and attribution defect produce step-specific advisory warnings; and the explicitly allowed readable overlap does not produce an overlap warning.
- Execution: Run in the repository's browser-backed integration suite on every pull request with Chromium available.
- Covers: Build failure, missing or malformed reference sample, runtime or console failure, failed step transition, and process-level failure reporting.
- Surface: `npm run verify` from controlled throwaway copies of the repository.
- Setup: Create independent disposable copies and introduce one representative fault per verification phase without changing the source checkout.
- Journey: Run verification against a build-breaking edit, a missing or out-of-order sample, a step that emits a browser error, and a transition that does not advance the public step index.

- Assertions: Every faulty copy exits non-zero; the output names the failed phase and, for browser or transition faults, the offending step; no failure is reported as success; and preview subprocesses are cleaned up after each run.
- Execution: Run in the repository's browser-backed end-to-end suite on every pull request with Chromium available.
### AT-003: Interact with the evolving reference scene across modes and viewports

- Covers: Nine-step scene continuity, grouped persistence, entering and departing entities, browse/present modes, navigation methods and boundaries, position preservation, active-state semantics, fixed-canvas scaling, attribution, and responsive visual composition.
- Actor and surface: A viewer uses the committed reference presentation in a production preview through `chrome-devtools-axi`.
- Setup: Build and serve the app on `127.0.0.1`; open the canonical sample at a wide desktop viewport, with a narrow viewport available for a second pass. No credentials are required.

- Steps: Inspect the first step; navigate by keyboard, progress control, table of contents, and representative horizontal touch swipe; attempt navigation before the first and after the last step; focus an interactive control and use its key behavior; toggle browse/present mode on a middle step and back; traverse all nine steps while inspecting continuing, entering, and departing entities; then repeat representative first, dense, and final steps at the narrow viewport.

- Expected: Every input reaches the intended step without wrapping or double-handling focused-control keys; direct jumps and semantic current-state hooks agree; mode changes preserve the active step and expose the specified chrome; grouped scenes update without whole-scene replacement, persisting entities morph in place, newcomers enter after continuing motion, and departing entities exit; the 880 × 380 composition scales without internal reflow; attribution is legible and linked; active chrome is distinct; and important content remains readable without accidental chrome collisions at both viewport widths.

- Evidence: Record an accessibility/DOM snapshot showing active semantics and attribution, step-index observations for every navigation method and boundary, and settled screenshots of the first, last, and dense or transition-critical steps in both wide and narrow views.
- Effects and cleanup: Only local preview and browser processes are authorized; stop them after evidence capture. No repository writes, credentials, publication, or paid effects.
- Permitted substitutes: Equivalent browser input synthesis may stand in for a physical touchscreen; DOM-only inspection may not replace the required settled screenshots or continuity observations.
